# GitHub Actions and S3 {.unnumbered} :::: {.callout-warning collapse='false' appearance='default' icon='false'} ## [Caution]{style='font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.25em;'} ::: {style='font-size: 1.00em; color: var(--callout-body-color, #282b2d);'} This chapter is under review. Thank you for your patience. ::: :::: GitHub Actions can automatically build and publish our `vetiver` models to our S3 whenever we push changes to a specific branch (we covered these in [Lab 5](lab05.qmd) and [GitHub Actions as CI/CD](publish-r-py.qmd)). I've stored the Quarto files for building, pushing, and pulling the model data in the [`_labs/lab07/` folder](https://github.com/mjfrigaard/do4ds-labs/tree/main/_labs/lab07). In this section I'll cover connecting GitHub to AWS with OpenID Connect (OIDC) and creating a workflow to automate the model publishing process. ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'GitHub Actions Automated Deployment' %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'look': 'classic', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace'}}}%% graph TD Push(["Developer

We could store the `mjfrigaard-cli` access key in the repository's secrets, but that key can do much more than this workflow needs. It carries every permission in `dev-deploy-group` (including `AmazonEC2FullAccess` and `IAMFullAccess`), it never expires, and our local `dev-deploy` profile uses the same key. If the secret leaked, someone could launch instances or create IAM users. Rotating the key ([Rotating access keys](start-aws.qmd#rotating-access-keys)) would also mean updating the laptop and GitHub at the same time. OIDC avoids storing a key at all. Each workflow run asks GitHub for a signed token that names the repository and branch it's running from. AWS checks the token and hands back temporary credentials for an IAM role, and those credentials expire after an hour. The role can only write to the model bucket, and only this repository's `lab07-s3` branch can assume it. ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'GitHub OIDC and AWS' %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'look': 'classic', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace'}}}%% graph TD Run(["Workflow Run
(lab07-s3)"]) Token("GitHub OIDC Token
repo + branch") STS("AWS STS

Credentials (1 hour)") Access[("Access to S3")] Run --"requests"--> Token Token --"AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity"--> STS STS --> Role Role --> Creds Creds --> Access style Run fill:#E8A33D,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Token fill:#1B2A41,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style STS fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Role fill:#D2562B,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Creds fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Access fill:#5B8C5A,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff ``` Setting this up takes three steps in AWS (an identity provider, a role, and a permissions policy) and two repository variables. The AWS commands use the `dev-deploy` profile, which has `IAMFullAccess` from [Stand up an EC2 instance](aws-ec2.qmd). ### Adding GitHub as an identity provider First we tell IAM to trust tokens signed by GitHub. We only do this once per AWS account: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} aws iam create-open-id-connect-provider \ --url https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \ --client-id-list sts.amazonaws.com \ --profile dev-deploy ``` ::: The output is the provider's ARN: ::: {style="font-style: italic;"} ```{.default} { "OpenIDConnectProviderArn": "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_ID:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com" } ``` ::: ### Creating the role The role's trust policy decides who can assume it. Store the account ID in a shell variable, then write the policy to `trust-policy.json`. Type `ACCOUNT_ID` exactly as written (don't replace it with your account number), because the shell fills in the number for us. Run both commands in the same Terminal session from the repository root: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} ACCOUNT_ID=$(aws sts get-caller-identity \ --query Account --output text \ --profile dev-deploy) cat > trust-policy.json <:role/gha-s3-publish-role`), which goes in the repository below. :::: {.callout-note collapse='false' appearance='default' icon='false'} ## [AWS Pager Output]{style='font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.25em;'} ::: {style='font-size: 1.00em; color: var(--callout-body-color, #282b2d);'} The output repeats because the AWS CLI sends long output through a pager (`less`), and each scroll redrew it. Press `q` to get back to the prompt. To turn the pager off for this session, run: ```bash export AWS_PAGER="" ``` ::: :::: ### Limiting the role to the model bucket The new role has no permissions. `pins` lists, reads, and writes objects in the bucket, so the permissions policy allows those three actions on `penguin-vetiver-model-data` and nothing else: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} cat > s3-publish-policy.json < **Secrets and variables** > **Actions** > **Variables**). Neither one is sensitive. The role ARN is useless outside the repository and branch named in the trust policy: 1. `AWS_ROLE_ARN`: the ARN of `gha-s3-publish-role` 2. `AWS_REGION`: AWS region (e.g., `us-east-1`) We can set both from the Terminal with the GitHub CLI (in the same shell, so `ACCOUNT_ID` is still set): ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} gh variable set AWS_ROLE_ARN \ --body "arn:aws:iam::${ACCOUNT_ID}:role/gha-s3-publish-role" ``` ::: ::: {style="font-style: italic;"} ```{.default} ✓ Created variable AWS_ROLE_ARN for mjfrigaard/do4ds-labs ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} gh variable set AWS_REGION --body "us-east-1" ``` ::: ::: {style="font-style: italic;"} ```{.default} ✓ Updated variable AWS_REGION for mjfrigaard/do4ds-labs ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} gh variable list ``` ::: ::: {style="font-style: italic;"} ```{.default} NAME VALUE UPDATED AWS_REGION us-east-1 less than a minute ago AWS_ROLE_ARN arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_ID:role/gha-s3-publish-role about 1 minute ago ``` ::: The repository doesn't need any AWS secrets. If it still has `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` from an earlier setup, delete them after the first successful run with the role: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} gh secret delete AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} gh secret delete AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY ``` ::: If a secret doesn't exist, `gh secret delete` returns a 404 error: ::: {style="font-style: italic;"} ```{.default} failed to delete secret AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: HTTP 404 (https://api.github.com/repos/mjfrigaard/do4ds-labs/actions/secrets/AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID) ``` ::: The 404 means there's nothing to delete, so we can ignore it. `gh secret list` confirms the repository has no secrets left (it prints nothing): ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} gh secret list ``` ::: ### GitHub Actions Workflow File Next, we create `.github/workflows/publish.yml`[^gha-workflow] to build and publish the models to our S3 bucket. The models are automatically versioned by `vetiver` (e.g., `20260710T065220Z-91fdd`), so we're creating a new version in S3 with each workflow run. ```{.yaml} name: Publish Models to S3 on: push: branches: [lab07-s3] #<1> paths: - '_labs/lab07/py_model.qmd' - '_labs/lab07/r_model.qmd' - '.github/workflows/publish.yml' permissions: #<2> id-token: write contents: read #<2> jobs: publish-models: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Check out repository #<3> uses: actions/checkout@v4 #<3> - name: Configure AWS credentials #<4> uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4 with: role-to-assume: ${{ vars.AWS_ROLE_ARN }} aws-region: ${{ vars.AWS_REGION || 'us-east-1' }} #<4> - name: Set up Python #<5> uses: actions/setup-python@v5 with: python-version: '3.12' - name: Set up R uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2 with: r-version: '4.4' use-public-rspm: true - name: Set up Quarto uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2 - name: Install Python dependencies working-directory: ./_labs/lab07 run: | python -m pip install --upgrade pip pip install -r Python/requirements.txt pins vetiver python-dotenv s3fs jupyter "setuptools<81" - name: Install R dependencies working-directory: ./_labs/lab07 run: | R -e "install.packages(c('vetiver', 'pins', 'plumber2', 'paws.storage', 'palmerpenguins', 'duckdb', 'DBI', 'dplyr', 'rmarkdown', 'knitr'))" #<5> - name: Build and publish Python model #<6> working-directory: ./_labs/lab07 env: USE_S3: 'true' AWS_REGION: ${{ vars.AWS_REGION || 'us-east-1' }} PINS_ALLOW_PICKLE_READ: '1' run: | quarto render py_model.qmd - name: Build and publish R model working-directory: ./_labs/lab07 env: USE_S3: 'true' AWS_REGION: ${{ vars.AWS_REGION || 'us-east-1' }} run: | quarto render r_model.qmd #<6> ``` 1. **Trigger**: Runs when `py_model.qmd`, `r_model.qmd`, or this workflow file changes on the `lab07-s3` branch 2. **Permissions**: `id-token: write` lets the job request an OIDC token from GitHub. Setting `permissions` removes the defaults, so `contents: read` keeps checkout working 3. **Checkout**: Downloads the latest code from the repository 4. **AWS Auth**: Uses `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials` to trade the OIDC token for temporary credentials from `gha-s3-publish-role` 5. **Setup**: Installs Python 3.12, R 4.4, Quarto, and the required dependencies 6. **Build & Publish**: Renders `py_model.qmd` and `r_model.qmd` with the `USE_S3=true` environment variable, which causes the model code to write directly to S3 The workflow renders the same `.qmd` files we render locally, so there are no separate scripts to keep in sync. The `use-public-rspm: true` option in the **Set up R** step points R at the [Posit Public Package Manager](https://p3m.dev/), which serves prebuilt Linux binaries. Without it, `install.packages()` compiles every R package from source, and the first successful run of this workflow took about 25 minutes (most of it in **Install R dependencies**). Publishing with GitHub Actions automates the model deployment without storing any AWS credentials in the repository. [^gha-workflow]: Note that file is stored in the [root directory (`.github/workflows/`)](https://github.com/mjfrigaard/do4ds-labs/tree/main/.github/workflows)--where all workflow files belong. ## Developing on the `lab07-s3` Branch Because I want the `main` branch reserved for the Quarto book rendering, I'll create and check out a `lab07-s3` branch from `main` for model changes (pushing to this branch triggers the model publishing workflow): ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} git checkout -b lab07-s3 ``` ::: And push the new branch to GitHub: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} git push -u origin lab07-s3 ``` ::: Once on the `lab07-s3` branch, I'll need to follow this process: ### Make changes Make changes to the model files (i.e., [`_labs/lab07/py_model.qmd`](https://github.com/mjfrigaard/do4ds-labs/blob/main/_labs/lab07/py_model.qmd) or [`_labs/lab07/r_model.qmd`](https://github.com/mjfrigaard/do4ds-labs/blob/main/_labs/lab07/r_model.qmd)) ### Test changes (locally) To test changes locally, I'll need to set the environment variables for S3 (or use local for testing): ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} export USE_S3=false # or true if testing S3 locally ``` ::: Then render/run the files with the changes ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} quarto render py_model.qmd ``` ::: Or ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} quarto render r_model.qmd ``` ::: ### Commit changes Commit the changes (be specific about the files): ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} git add _labs/lab07/py_model.qmd _labs/lab07/r_model.qmd git commit -m "Update model configuration or training logic" ``` ::: ### Push changes Push to the `lab07-s3` branch: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} git push origin lab07-s3 ``` ::: GitHub Actions will automatically detect the `push` to `lab07-s3`, build the models using the latest code, and publish the versioned models to S3 with temporary credentials from `gha-s3-publish-role`. ### Verify The GitHub CLI (`gh`) lets us follow the workflow from the Terminal. First, list the most recent runs of `publish.yml`. Each row shows the status, the commit message, the branch, the run ID, and how long the run took: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} gh run list --workflow publish.yml --limit 2 ``` ::: Pass the run ID from that list to `gh run watch` to follow the run until it finishes. The `--exit-status` flag makes the command fail when the run fails, so we don't have to read the output to know the result: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} gh run watch --exit-status ``` ::: To confirm the run used the role (and not an access key), search the **Configure AWS credentials** step in the run's log: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} gh run view --log | grep -i -m5 "assum\|gha-s3-publish-role" ``` ::: ::: {style="font-style: italic;"} ```{.default} publish-models Configure AWS credentials 2026-11-15T05:41:59.5159429Z role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_ID:role/gha-s3-publish-role publish-models Configure AWS credentials 2026-11-15T05:41:59.9075276Z Assuming role with OIDC publish-models Configure AWS credentials 2026-11-15T05:42:00.1552995Z Authenticated as assumedRoleId ROLE_ID:GitHubActions ``` ::: `Assuming role with OIDC` means GitHub traded its token for temporary credentials, and `GitHubActions` is the session name the action gives the role. If the role is missing an S3 permission, the build steps fail with `AccessDenied`, so we also check that the log has none (`0` means no matches): ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} gh run view --log | grep -i -c "accessdenied\|not authorized" ``` ::: ::: {style="font-style: italic;"} ```{.default} 0 ``` ::: To see where the time goes, `gh api` requests the run's jobs from the GitHub REST API (`{owner}` and `{repo}` are filled in from the current repository). The `--jq` filter prints each step's name and how many seconds it took. The **Install R dependencies** step should take about a minute with `use-public-rspm: true` (compiling from source took most of the 25 minute first run): ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs//jobs \ --jq '.jobs[0].steps[] | "\(.name): \(((.completed_at|fromdate)-(.started_at|fromdate)))s"' ``` ::: We can also confirm R downloaded its packages from Package Manager by searching the run's log for its address (`packagemanager.posit.co`). The `__linux__` part of each URL means Package Manager sends a prebuilt binary for the runner's Linux version: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} gh run view --log | grep -m3 "packagemanager.posit.co" ``` ::: Finally, we verify the models were published by listing the files in the bucket. Each run adds a new version folder (named with the date and time, e.g., `20261106T183259Z-6a79d`) under `Python/models/penguin_lab07_model/` and `R/models/penguin_lab07_model/`: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} # List files in S3 aws s3 ls s3://penguin-vetiver-model-data/ --recursive --profile dev-deploy ``` ::: ### Merge to `main` Then switch back to the `main` branch: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} git checkout main ``` ::: This will merge the changes in `lab07-s3` to `main` (if the changes also belong in the book). ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} git merge lab07-s3 ``` ::: Push changes to `main`. ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} git push origin main ``` ::: Then publish the book: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} quarto publish gh-pages ``` ::: ## Recap 1. GitHub authenticates to AWS with OIDC instead of an access key. We added GitHub as an identity provider and created `gha-s3-publish-role`, which only the `lab07-s3` branch of this repository can assume and which can only list, read, and write objects in the model bucket. The role ARN and `AWS_REGION` go in the repository's Variables, and each run gets credentials that expire after an hour. 2. `publish.yml` runs on pushes to the `lab07-s3` branch that change `py_model.qmd`, `r_model.qmd`, or the workflow file itself. It installs Python and R, then renders both model documents with `USE_S3=true`, so each run writes a new `vetiver` version to S3. 3. Model changes happen on `lab07-s3` (make changes, test locally, commit, push, and verify with `aws s3 ls`), which keeps `main` reserved for rendering the book. Changes that also belong in the book get merged back into `main`. [Lab 8](lab08.qmd) moves to the command line and how SSH keys work.
